    It is therefore my happy privilege, as a representative of our Government in the capacity of Administrative Field Officer of Works Progress Administration, Dallas Areas No. 4, to now dedicate this building in the spirit of this poem, to serve for all time to come the welfare of the young and old— as a place of wholesome learning and wholesome recreation, may be developed into a community center in all that the term means and, as such, inspire and encourage to nobler thinking and higher ambition in life all who may enjoy its benefits, and I now so dedicate it.


ACCEPTANCE ADDRESS ON BEHALF OF THE FOUNDERS

By Mrs. Annie Halsell Woodward

    Mr. Chairman, Ladies, and Gentlemen:

    Little did I ever think that the day would come in my life when I would stand here to pay public tribute to my father—my beloved father—Warren Halsell. It is with deep appreciation that I am permitted to be here today, and while many of you know of him by the gracious acts he performed and the noble things he stood for, I knew him as a loving and tender father, with all the meaning that implies, and therefore well realize the feeling that is in my heart today as I speak. None of the other children of his are present, my taking part, in some small way, in paying tribute to the memory of him was first and foremost the reason for being here today.

    It seems to us, in whose veins courses his blood, that today we stand on the threshold of a greater era. It is out of a century that he dedicated some of the best years of his life to the service of his fellow-man, and it was most fitting that here, where he gave gratefully his best efforts to know and that men making a school in this little town and in this county, a place of service, for in serving others he had in mind the knowledge of living.

    If there could be gathered a roll of those who were at one time or another his pupils, there would be found embodied in that list a large number of those who have become leaders in their respective communities and who, the servants of their fellow men—men who became leaders in all that stood for better life in the community, the county, in the society in which they move and have their being.
